This paper introduces a time-dependent Poisson autoregressive model, termed TDPAR, designed to capture both temporal dynamics and potential structural shifts in count data. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of a new estimator, the time-dependent generalized Yule-Walker (TDGYW), for TDPAR. Furthermore, we develop a consistent estimator for the change-point within the autoregressive coefficient and propose a testing procedure to detect structural breaks in the Poisson mean. Simulation studies demonstrate that TDPAR effectively identifies structural changes in both the mean and autoregressive coefficient, outperforming standard Poisson autoregressive models. The utility of TDPAR is illustrated using daily Twitter volume data related to the 2016 US presidential election. Supplementary materials, including additional simulation results, further details on the 2016 election data analysis, and the R code for implementing TDPAR, are available online.

This study introduces a novel technique for monitoring atmospheric optical depth ($\tau$) at specific altitudes by analyzing the photometric light curves of stars obscured by clouds. The method relies on the assumption that cloud tops exhibit uniform brightness, allowing the extraction of $\tau$ from the amplitude of dips in the light curve caused by stellar photons passing through the atmosphere above the clouds. We validated this approach using photometric data from 17 stars observed by the TROPOS stellar monitor in Aspendale, Australia, and concurrent lidar measurements from the same site. The resulting $\tau$ values were compared against those derived from the vertical aerosol profile measured by the lidar, assuming a constant aerosol layer with uniform brightness. The correlation coefficient between the new method and the lidar-derived values was 0.71, with a root-mean-square difference of 0.12. Furthermore, the light curve data enabled the detection of discrete aerosol layers, which were subsequently identified in the corresponding lidar profiles. This technique offers a low-cost, high-temporal-resolution alternative to lidar for measuring optical depth, provided that suitable stars and cloud cover are available. Its primary applications include the calibration of remote sensing instruments and the evaluation of global climate models. The method is detailed in Section 2, with observational data and results presented in Sections 3 and 4, respectively. Concluding remarks are offered in Section 5.

Sampling methods for Bayesian inference in molecular dynamics are crucial for exploring high-dimensional configurational spaces. This study introduces a novel, robust, and efficient Langevin dynamics algorithm designed to accelerate configurational sampling. The proposed approach employs a hybrid integrator that combines the standard Verlet integrator with a fast, high-order integrator applied to a subset of harmonic oscillators within a normal mode transformation. This combination yields a significant reduction in the global integration error, thereby allowing for larger timesteps and faster sampling. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by accelerating sampling in a complex, realistic system: the folding of the Trp-cage peptide. Compared to conventional Langevin dynamics, our approach achieves a 100-fold increase in sampling speed with a timestep of 20 femtoseconds, and a 200-fold acceleration with a 15 femtosecond timestep. These results indicate that the new method is both sturdy and efficient, capable of maintaining high acceptance rates even with large timesteps across various systems. The algorithm is implemented in AMBER, CHARMM, GROMACS, NAMD, and OpenMM. Detailed implementation specifics are provided for AMBER, with applicable modifications required for other packages. The implementation for AMBER is accessible at https://github.com/yang-lab/AMDyn.

This study introduces the creation of a smaller, high-quality reference dataset derived from existing image description data, intended for evaluating automatic image description systems. We demonstrate how this dataset can be utilized to assess systems that rely on human benchmark data for evaluation. Furthermore, we present findings from applying this dataset to the WICCap data to develop a specialized, high-quality reference set. Finally, we report results on using this refined dataset to evaluate descriptions generated by neural models against the original Wikipedia-based references. This study examines the baryon-to-meson ratio, a quantity that remains constant during the hydrodynamic phase of heavy-ion collisions. By analyzing recent data from Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV, we observe that the baryon-to-pion ratio in central Au+Au events is approximately a factor of two higher than in p+Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=5.02$ TeV. Based on this finding, we forecast that in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=100$ TeV, the baryon-to-meson ratio will fall below unity. Consequently, the yield of mesons will surpass that of baryons at both the initial stage and during the final state of proton-proton interactions at 100 TeV. These results indicate that baryon production will exceed meson production at the chemical freeze-out temperature for pp collisions at 100 TeV, a trend that aligns with predictions from hadron resonance gas models. We further anticipate that the baryon-to-meson ratio in proton-air collisions at 100 TeV will remain below unity, a characteristic shared with proton-proton collisions at the same energy. This ratio is expected to be independent of the impact parameter in both pp and p-Ar systems. Finally, we propose that the baryon-to-meson ratio in air-air collisions at 100 TeV will also be less than one, potentially serving as a defining characteristic for such events. These conclusions are derived from a comprehensive framework that integrates parton energy loss, hydrodynamics, and hadron resonance gas models. The framework incorporates the chemical potentials for baryon number, strangeness, and charge, alongside the mass and chemical equilibrium fractions of hadron resonance species. Additionally, it accounts for the conversion of quark-gluon plasma to hadrons, hadron chemistry, and the freeze-out of hadronic species. This approach enables the prediction of baryon and meson yields in both pp and A-A collisions at 100 TeV. The framework is also applicable to other systems, including heavy-ion collisions at lower energies and neutron star mergers. Ultimately, the baryon-to-meson ratio offers a valuable observable for investigating hadron production across a wide range of systems and energies.

This paper introduces the concept of integrated data and energy delivery (IDED) over single- and multi-carrier orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems. We formulate an optimization problem aimed at maximizing total data rate while satisfying minimum data and power harvesting constraints for users. By transforming the IDED-OFDM problem into its equivalent wideband counterpart, we develop a globally optimal solution using iterative waterfilling. For the single-carrier IDED-OFDM scenario, we propose a low-complexity near-optimal algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the wideband IDED system significantly outperforms single- and multi-carrier OFDM approaches. Furthermore, the performance gains of the IDEED systems surpass those observed in wideband MISO broadcast systems. The proposed single-carrier and wideband solutions offer a valuable benchmark for evaluating other sub-optimal methods in large-scale single- and multi-carrier OFDM deployments. Ultimately, the findings indicate that the benefits of multiple carriers in OFDM systems are limited, and the advantages of IDEED systems stem primarily from the inclusion of energy harvesting constraints rather than the use of multiple carriers. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) demands a comprehensive theoretical framework that integrates diverse data sources, ranging from high-precision low-energy measurements to high-energy data with significant theoretical uncertainties. This framework must also accommodate various parametrisation and regularisation schemes. We present a Python-based framework designed to unify these elements, enabling the exploration of numerous fitting strategies. The framework incorporates a wide array of data sources, including recent PDF sets, global fits, and specific data sets. It supports multiple parametrisation forms and orders, as well as various regularisation schemes such as $\overline{\text{MS}}$, AC, and CMW. Furthermore, it accounts for scale-dependent theoretical uncertainties via Hessian and Monte Carlo methods, as well as non-perturbative uncertainties. We demonstrate the framework's capabilities by fitting a simple PDF using distinct strategies and regularisation schemes, and by analysing the impact of theoretical uncertainties from different data sets on the resulting PDF. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AMehta27/PDF_Fitting_Framework.

This study employs a linearized framework to model the response of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic forcing via an active flame approach. The linearized governing equations are derived for both the precombustion flow and the reacting flow, with the latter formulated as a combination of linearized and nonlinear components. The nonlinear terms are represented through a flame response function, which is determined by fitting the linearized model to direct numerical simulation data. The resulting model accurately reproduces the vorticity and heat release fluctuations observed in the simulations. Furthermore, it captures the variation in heat release fluctuation amplitude across different azimuthal wavenumbers, aligning well with simulation results. Finally, the model's predictions for heat release fluctuations are compared against those from a linearized eddy-breakup model. These findings demonstrate that the proposed model effectively replicates the heat release fluctuations of the simulated turbulent jet flame, thereby offering a valuable tool for investigating flame-vortex interactions and instabilities in turbulent flames. Ultimately, this linearized model serves as a practical framework for analyzing heat release fluctuations in turbulent jet flames under various operating conditions. The governing equations and associated boundary conditions are detailed in Section 2, while Section 3 describes the determination of the flame response function. Section 4 presents the results, and Section 5 offers the study's conclusions. The symbols utilized in this work are listed in Table 1.

Nonlocal gravity represents a recent extension of Einstein's general relativity, formulated within the framework of Poincaré-invariant nonlocal field theories. This approach incorporates an infinite sequence of local, nonderivative operators that generate nonlocal effects. These operators are constructed from fundamental frames, which are tensorial structures analogous to the metric tensor. In this work, we introduce a specific nonlocal gravity model grounded in the Einstein-Aether fundamental frame. We derive the constitutive relation linking the nonlocal curvature tensor to the fundamental frames and derive the nonlocal Einstein field equations. Furthermore, we propose a simplified local approximation of these nonlocal equations and demonstrate that this approximation aligns with recent nonlocal gravity models. Finally, we establish the local nonlocal gravity model's compatibility with recent theories of modified gravity.

The study of rare, low-multiplicity final states at hadron colliders serves as a powerful probe for new physics, offering high sensitivity to heavy new particles through deviations in angular distributions. This paper provides an overview of the search for minor systems—specifically central diffractive events, single and double pomeron exchange, and central exclusive production—at the LHC. It details the associated experimental challenges and outlines the current status of these investigations at ATLAS and CMS. Furthermore, it examines the potential for other LHC experiments to explore these processes and highlights the future prospects for central diffractive and exclusive physics at high-luminosity colliders.

The variable luminosity of Sgr A* and the existence of a cluster of Galactic Centre (GC) X-ray binaries in quiescence raise the question of why no transient neutron star (NS) low-mass X-ray binary (LMXB) has been detected in this region. We demonstrate that the mean recurrence interval for NS LMXBs in the GC exceeds 100 years, a duration that aligns with the age of the GC LMXB population and suggests they have been present since the GC was a star-forming environment. Furthermore, we argue that the two GC NS LMXBs currently in quiescence, XTE J1739-285 and 4U 1728-34, are likely to experience X-ray outbursts within the coming decade, potentially resolving the mystery surrounding their detection. Finally, we contend that a recently identified millisecond radio pulsar in the GC, PSR J1745-2900, is a NS LMXB in a persistent low-luminosity state, a conclusion supported by an estimated mass accretion rate of $\sim 10^{-10}$ M$_{\sun}$ yr$^{-1}$ derived from X-ray and radio observations. This finding implies that the GC is home to at least three such systems, offering valuable insights into the evolution of NS LMXBs. These systems may also represent a significant component of the NS population responsible for the gravitational wave events detected by LIGO and Virgo. Additionally, we address the origin of the recently reported radio emission from the neutron star in 4U 1728-34, proposing a mechanism for its generation. Throughout this discussion, we highlight several open questions regarding the Galactic Centre's neutron star population. To support these arguments, we provide a table summarizing the properties of all known GC X-ray binaries and a figure illustrating the recurrence intervals of outbursts for various NS LMXBs.

Bipartite graphs represent vertices and edges as tasks and resources, respectively, to model scheduling problems. A central challenge in this area is determining whether a given bipartite graph $G=(V,E)$ admits a valid edge coloring using $k$ colors, a problem known to be NP-complete. This study introduces a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm that decides if a bipartite graph $G=(V,E)$ is $k$-colorable based on the parameter $p$, defined as the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve $k$-colorability. The algorithm runs in $O(2.326^{p} \cdot |V|^{2} \cdot |E|)$ time. Furthermore, if the graph is found to be $p$-splittable, the method constructs a split graph $G^{*}$ with $|V^{*}| = |V| + |E|$ vertices and $|E^{*}| = |V| \cdot |E|$ edges, ensuring $G^{*}$ is $K_{2, k+1}$-free. This result yields an improved approximation ratio for the edge chromatic number of the original graph $G$. The proposed FPT algorithm for testing splittability and the resulting splittability-based coloring technique are applicable to any bipartite graph. Numerical examples demonstrate that this splittability-based approach can surpass current best-known bounds for specific graphs. This paper introduces HyperDegrade, a system designed to extend the runtime of computationally intensive tasks by dynamically reducing CPU frequency. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on aggressive voltage scaling, HyperDegrade maintains the CPU at its maximum frequency while managing runtime through cycles of rapid frequency drops and quick recoveries. These cycles are optimized based on the specific workload and hardware constraints. Evaluation using a diverse set of workloads demonstrates that HyperDegrade can prolong runtime by up to 2.1×, achieving energy savings comparable to traditional methods. Crucially, it delivers these benefits without increasing runtime, even for workloads that are already optimized for low frequencies. Additionally, the approach offers significant runtime extensions for workloads that cannot be effectively slowed via voltage scaling. Beyond prolonging runtime, HyperDegrade enables other energy-saving strategies, such as shutting down idle cores, to further reduce power consumption. The system is implemented entirely in userspace, requiring no kernel modifications or hardware changes. Source code is available at https://github.com/Pranav-1999/HyperDegrade.

This paper addresses the problem of synchronizing two tasks across a team of robots operating on a regular graph, where the tasks are defined by a pair of functions. We formulate the task synchronization challenge as a strategic game between a team of robots and an adversary, with the objective of minimizing the final error. The robots are constrained by limited communication and computation capabilities, while the adversary is restricted by a budget for modifying the graph's topology. We propose a decentralized algorithm for the robots that leverages the graph's regularity and remains robust against topological changes caused by the adversary. Simulation results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AmirhosseinNajafi/Multi-TaskSynchronization.

This paper introduces a Cartesian Breakdown Approach designed to embed direct products of groups into wreath products. Utilizing this method, we demonstrate that the direct power $T^n$ of a finite monomial transformation group $T$ embeds into the direct product $S_m \times S_m \cdots \times S_m$ ($n$ times), where $m = \left\lceil \frac{3}{2} \log_2 n \right\rceil + 2$. Consequently, we establish that $T^n$ embeds into the $m$-fold wreath product $T \wr T \wr \cdots \wr T$ ($m$ times). As a direct application of these findings, we derive an explicit upper bound for the rank of the monomial transformation group $T_n$ acting on the set $[n] \times [n]$, showing that $rank(T_n) \leq 2^{\sqrt{2n} + O(1)}$. Furthermore, we provide an explicit construction of a rank-2 monomial transformation group on $[n] \times [n]$ with an infinite diameter, which serves as a counterexample to a conjecture by A. Ash, S. Thomas, and A. Viswanath regarding the diameter of groups with limited rank. Alongside this construction, we also present an explicit formulation for calculating the diameter of groups with rank $r$ acting on the set $[n] \times [n]$. Finally, we apply our results to determine the rank of various specific monomial transformation groups defined on $[n] \times [n]$.

The high-frequency sensitivity of current gravitational-wave detectors is constrained by optical shot noise, a limitation that can be addressed by increasing circulating light power through novel interferometer topologies. This study examines the sloshing Sagnac interferometer (SSI), a configuration that utilizes a single Fabry-Perot cavity to achieve high power buildup. We present a comprehensive model of the SSI's response to gravitational waves and derive an analytical expression for its sensitivity curve. Furthermore, we propose an optimized design for third-generation detectors and evaluate its performance against both realistic first- and second-generation instruments as well as other proposed third-generation concepts. Our analysis indicates that an optimally configured sloshing Sagnac interferometer could surpass the sensitivity of advanced LIGO by up to an order of magnitude across a broad frequency range, potentially offering a cost-effective solution for future gravitational-wave observatories. Detailed specifications for this optimal setup are provided in Table 1. Ultimately, we assess the detectability of known gravitational-wave sources using this configuration.

Extra-large scale massive multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems are anticipated to serve ultra-dense user distributions in future ultra-high capacity scenarios, such as smart cities. These systems rely on random access (RA) protocols to manage user connections without requiring prior knowledge of user locations. This paper examines the non-intersecting visibility regions (NIRs) among access points (APs) within an XL-MIMO RA protocol. By analyzing the impact of NIRs on RA performance, we introduce a simplified model that accounts for these regions. Utilizing this model, we derive the probability distribution of visible APs per user and the corresponding distribution of RA pilot collisions. Based on these distributions, we formulate the spectral efficiency (SE) and sum-SE, which are then optimized through a two-step approach: first, by determining the optimal number of pilot sequences per AP, and second, by optimizing the power allocation between access and data phases. Numerical results demonstrate that incorporating NIRs into the XL-MIMO RA protocol yields significant performance gains. Furthermore, the proposed NIR-aware protocol achieves higher sum-SE than existing state-of-the-art solutions across various user densities. To validate these findings, Monte Carlo simulations are conducted to confirm the accuracy of our analytical results. The study concludes with a discussion on potential future research directions regarding NIRs in XL-MIMO systems. The key notation used throughout this work is summarized in Table I. Our analysis reveals that the NIRs between APs are significant in extra-large scale deployments, and accounting for them can substantially enhance system performance. Consequently, future XL-MIMO systems should integrate NIR-aware protocols to maximize spectral efficiency. This paper provides a comprehensive investigation into the non-intersecting visibility regions between APs and their positive impact on XL-MIMO system performance. We propose an NIR-aware RA protocol that improves spectral efficiency and verifies its superiority over conventional RA methods. The detailed description of the system model and the formulation of optimization problems follow in the subsequent section.

Neural language models have largely supplanted $n$-gram models in recent years due to their superior performance on standard tasks. This shift is driven by the fact that neural models effectively capture complex linguistic patterns, a capability that $n$-gram approaches struggle with because of their limited context window and reliance on local statistics. In this study, we demonstrate that a simple $n$-gram model, when trained with a recently proposed distribution matching objective, can match or even surpass the quality of state-of-the-art neural models. Building on this finding, we introduce a hybrid framework that leverages the strengths of both approaches: a deep neural network learns residual errors from a high-order $n$-gram model. Empirical results show that this method significantly outperforms purely neural baselines across multiple text generation tasks, including machine translation, language modeling, and abstract writing. Furthermore, the approach offers substantial computational advantages, requiring approximately 100 times less memory and 10 times fewer parameters than current state-of-the-art models. These gains are achieved without compromising generation quality, as measured by perplexity, BLEU, and human evaluation. We anticipate that this framework will facilitate the deployment of high-quality language models in resource-constrained environments. The source code is available at: https://github.com/linguistojan/Ngram-Residual-Learning.

This study introduces Informed OCR (iOCR), a system designed to enhance the accuracy of image-based text extraction for election ballot tallies. The approach begins by identifying the source of each tally image, such as a specific ballot or scan, and then selects the most suitable OCR engine based on that context. Additionally, the system leverages contextual information from neighboring pixels and characters to correct recognition errors. Evaluation using a dataset of 100,000 ballot images from the 2020 US general election demonstrates that iOCR achieves higher accuracy than existing image-based methods. When integrated with traditional character-based tallies, the resulting hybrid approach surpasses both standalone image-based and character-based methods in accuracy. Furthermore, iOCR is compatible with various open-source image-based tallying tools, including BallotParser, BallotTally, and BallotCleaner. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/UCF-DataMining/iOCR.

This study examines the atmospheric circulation patterns of terrestrial planets using simplified 2D global circulation models (GCMs). We employ a combination of Lagrangian and Eulerian analyses to investigate the evolution of circulation regimes as a function of rotation rate, thermal forcing, and planetary radius. Our results indicate that the circulation regime is primarily governed by the ratio of planetary radius to the Rossby deformation radius. Specifically, slowly rotating planets with Rossby numbers (Ro) less than one exhibit baroclinic turbulence, whereas rapidly rotating planets with Ro greater than one display cyclostrophic turbulence. For planets with Ro exceeding one, a transition from baroclinic to cyclostrophic turbulence occurs as the ratio of planetary radius to Rossby deformation radius increases. We further identify that the onset of cyclostrophic turbulence is marked by the emergence of large-scale, coherent, super-rotating vortices. These findings offer insights into the atmospheric circulation of extrasolar planets and assist in selecting appropriate models for data inversion. Additionally, these results provide a framework for understanding the circulation regimes of gas giant planets, potentially resolving long-standing issues regarding their atmospheric dynamics. The GCM code utilized in this work is accessible at https://github.com/rajeshksharma/GCM.

This paper presents a novel integral representation for the reciprocal Gamma function, $\Gamma(z)^{-1}$, derived through the regularization of a classical formula originally proposed by Ramanujan. We demonstrate that this new expression is amenable to numerical evaluation and can be employed to compute $\Gamma(z)^{-1}$ across the entire complex plane. Furthermore, we establish a regularized integral form for the product $\Gamma(a)^{-1}\Gamma(b)^{-1}$, which facilitates the derivation of a regularized integral for the Riemann zeta function. Finally, we explore the application of this last result in calculating high-order derivatives of $\zeta(s)$ at negative integers.

Hydrodynamic models serve as valuable tools for simulating quantum fluids, particularly in scenarios where solving the full quantum description is computationally impractical. These simulations are especially useful for investigating non-equilibrium dynamics in spatially extended systems. In this study, we introduce a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach termed Phase-space Random Hydrodynamics (QRH). This method integrates the Wigner function with hydrodynamic equations, offering a non-perturbative framework that accounts for inter-particle interactions. We apply QRH to simulate the non-equilibrium evolution of a trapped, interacting Bose gas following the sudden removal of confinement. The simulations reveal that inter-particle interactions significantly influence both global and local dynamics. Specifically, interactions facilitate the global transition from ballistic to hydrodynamic behavior and accelerate local expansion by generating an effective pressure. Furthermore, the simulations demonstrate that QRH accurately reproduces the dynamics predicted by the Gross-Pitaevskii equation under conditions of weak interactions. Finally, we observe that both the QRH and the stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii method yield comparable local dynamics, although they differ in their global behavior. The QRH simulations also provide insights into the system's entanglement entropy, indicating that inter-particle interactions slow its growth. Overall, the QRH framework proves effective for simulating quantum fluids with weak to moderate interactions, potentially serving as a practical alternative to other quantum hydrodynamic methods like the stochastic Gross-Pitaevskii approach. Given its foundation in the Wigner function, QRH can be applied to a wide range of quantum many-body systems, including fermionic ones. Ultimately, these simulations underscore the critical role of inter-particle interactions in driving non-equilibrium dynamics within quantum fluids. This survey introduces the Instructor-Student architecture, a framework designed for knowledge learning in artificial intelligence. Within this architecture, an instructor model generates predictions and corresponding rationales, which are then utilized to train a student model. The instructor can be a teacher network, a pre-trained model, or a combination of both. The student model learns from the instructor's predictions and associated rationales, potentially using the same rationales for other tasks. We examine the literature on this architecture, detailing how the instructor and student models are constructed, the learning objectives employed, and the specific knowledge learning tasks addressed. Furthermore, we discuss the advantages and limitations of the Instructor-Student architecture, propose potential future research directions, and provide an open-source implementation of this framework. The source code for this survey is accessible at: https://github.com/Abhishek-1998/Instructor-Student-Architecture-for-Knowledge-Learning-A-Survey.

This paper introduces a novel function representation designed to accelerate exact inference in graphical models, with specific applications to finding the optimal constrained path between two nodes and the most probable edge between two nodes under constraints. We demonstrate that this new representation accelerates the computation of variable and factor tables by a factor of $O(\min\{n,d\})$, where $n$ represents the number of nodes and $d$ denotes the maximum degree of a node. Leveraging this representation, we develop a dynamic programming algorithm for the most probable constrained path problem that achieves linear time complexity with respect to the length of the constraint list. Furthermore, we introduce a dynamic programming algorithm for the most probable edge problem that remains polynomial in the graph size and linear in the length of the constraint list. Extensive experiments conducted on both synthetic and real datasets confirm the effectiveness of this function representation and the proposed algorithms. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Funx.

We introduce a novel Hilbert-Poincaré sequence for the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of the diagonal embedding of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ within $\mathfrak{sl}_{n+1}$. This sequence serves as a concrete manifestation of the challenge in defining Hilbert series for infinite-dimensional Lie algebras. Leveraging this sequence, we demonstrate that the Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ aligns with the dimension of the $n$-th level of the (extended) Racah algebra $\mathcal{R}_n$. Furthermore, we establish that the Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial for $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ corresponds to the dimension of the (extended) Racah algebra $\mathcal{R}_n$. As a consequence, we derive the Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial for $\mathcal{R}_n$, thereby confirming that the (extended) Racah algebra $\mathcal{R}_n$ constitutes a finite-type Kac-Moody Lie algebra. Finally, we show that the Hilbert-Poincaré polynomial of $\mathcal{R}_n$ matches the dimension of the $n$-th level of the centralizer $Z(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of the diagonal embedding of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ inside the affine Kac-Moody Lie algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{sl}}_{n+1}$. Consequently, we conclude that the centralizer $Z(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ within the affine Kac-Moody Lie algebra $\hat{\mathfrak{sl}}_{n+1}$ is a finite-type Kac-Moody Lie algebra. These findings are derived through an explicit construction of the (extended) Racah algebra $\mathcal{R}_n$ as a quotient of the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, utilizing the Weyl algebra $A_1$. Our approach relies on the free Lie algebra $L(X)$ generated by a countable set $X$ and its associated Hilbert-Poincaré sequence, which we also explicitly construct. Significance testing represents a standard approach for evaluating whether the performance differences between two machine learning systems are statistically meaningful. This study introduces a refined paired-permutation testing framework designed to achieve precise p-values for structured test statistics, thereby reducing the number of trials required to reach a specified precision level. We demonstrate the utility of this method through a case study on the structural evaluation of sentence-ordering algorithms for statistical machine translation. The findings indicate that our approach is approximately ten times more sample-efficient than existing methods, such as the bootstrap and Monte Carlo techniques. The implementation of this method is accessible via the recently released structural evaluation toolkit, StruXEval, at https://github.com/StruXEval/StruXEval. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/robertulman/paired-permutation-testing.

The anisotropic flow of charged particles, specifically $v_2$ and $v_3$, was examined across centralities in Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}$ = 200 GeV using a multiphase transport model (AMPT). The results indicate that the initial anisotropy of the particle momentum distribution, $\epsilon$, is the dominant factor influencing anisotropic flow, with the medium's response governed by the speed of sound. Furthermore, the $v_3/p_T$ distribution in Au+Au collisions exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with respect to centrality, a feature that aligns with hydrodynamic model predictions. Additionally, the ratio of $v_3/v_2$ in Au+Au collisions is found to be lower than in Cu+Cu collisions, a trend that mirrors the observed ellipticity ratio $\epsilon_2/\epsilon_3$ across different centralities. These findings suggest that the initial geometry of the collision system is the primary determinant of anisotropic flow, with the medium's response dependent on the local energy density. Ultimately, the $v_3$ in Au+Au and $v_2$ in Cu+Cu collisions serve as signatures of the initial geometric anisotropy, reflecting the collective behavior of the quark-gluon plasma formed in heavy-ion collisions. The anisotropic flow $v_n$ is defined as $\langle \cos(n\phi-\Psi_n)\rangle$, where $\phi$ represents the azimuthal angle of the particle and $\Psi_n$ denotes the $n$-th order reaction plane angle.

This paper introduces a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter that models the birth process on a grid, specifically designed for sensor networks with a limited number of sensors. The proposed PMBM filter incorporates a novel birth process that combines a deterministic point process on a grid with a stochastic process governing the birth locations. Simulation results demonstrate that the new PMBM filter with the partially grid-based origin model outperforms conventional multi-target tracking filters in terms of both birth location estimation accuracy and overall target tracking accuracy. Furthermore, the study includes sensor management simulations to illustrate the practical applications of the proposed PMBM filter with the partially grid-based origin model. These simulations indicate that the new filter achieves higher target tracking accuracy than traditional approaches when sensors are scarce. The source code for the simulations is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/PMBM_filter_with_partially_grid_based_origin_model.

Soccer, a globally popular sport, has recently attracted significant attention from the data science community, leading to numerous studies on prediction and optimization tasks. While soccer is inherently stochastic, teams often face high-pressure moments where a single decision can determine victory or defeat. In these critical situations, players must act rationally to maximize their team's utility. This work introduces a novel deep reinforcement learning framework designed to improve decision-making during such pivotal moments. Our approach employs a two-stage method: first, a classifier identifies whether a game has entered a critical phase, and second, a policy network learns optimal actions specifically for those situations. Extensive experiments conducted on a real-world soccer dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms existing baselines. Furthermore, the learned policies offer valuable insights into player behavior within these high-stakes scenarios. The source code for this project is available at: https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/CRS_soccer.

This study introduces a single-point laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) setup capable of generating two-dimensional (2D) vibration data through distant operation. By integrating a 2D image sensor, the system tracks the LDV's optical spot across the target surface, enabling 2D vibration mapping without requiring mechanical movement of the LDV. The configuration employs a 100-mW HeNe laser, and the resulting 2D vibration data are derived from the Doppler frequency shifts of the LDV signal. Experimental results demonstrate that the LDV spot can be followed over a 0.6 m × 0.6 m area at a distance of 3.5 m, with a spatial resolution of 1.5 mm. The measured 2D vibration data align closely with those obtained from a scanning LDV system, confirming the accuracy of the proposed approach. These findings indicate that a single LDV unit can cover a large measurement area at a distance, offering a cost-effective solution for 2D vibration analysis.

This study examines the linear and nonlinear spectral characteristics, along with orbital stability, of ground state solutions for the one-dimensional Klein--Gordon equation coupled with an anharmonic oscillator potential. The analysis begins with a detailed investigation of the operator defining the equation's spectrum. Subsequently, the spectral and orbital stability of ground states are thoroughly examined. The findings indicate that nonlinear spectral instability is a universal feature for anharmonic potentials where the mass at infinity is lower than the initial mass. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that spectral instability at the positive eigenvalue $\mu_1$ corresponds directly to linear and nonlinear orbital instability of the ground state. Finally, the research explores the existence of excited states and their associated spectral and orbital stability properties. These results are significant for understanding the long-term dynamical behavior of solutions. The work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China under Grants No. 11971220 and No. 12071187. The authors also acknowledge the support of the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities.

At Belle II, the search for $B^+ \to K^+ (\gamma \gamma)_{\rm osc}$ decays serves a dual purpose: it enables precision tests of the Standard Model by measuring $B$ meson oscillations into neutrinoless double-meson states, and it opens direct avenues for investigating neutrinoless oscillations of Beyond-Standard-Model particles, specifically Majorana neutrinos and axion-like particles (ALPs). If the signal region for $B^+ \to K^+ (\gamma \gamma)_{\rm osc}$ remains empty at Belle II, we will establish an upper limit on the branching ratio for $B^+ \to K^+ \eta_1^{(m)}$, where $\eta_1^{(m)}$ represents a hidden-sector pseudoscalar with mass $m$. This limit will constrain the $B$-meson mixing amplitude involving ALPs, $A(B\to\eta_1)$, to approximately $1.5\times 10^{-2}$ for $m=500$ MeV. Such a constraint would surpass the sensitivity of direct searches at LHCb and future experiments like FCC-ee and CEPC. Furthermore, the reach of $A(B\to\eta_1)$ at colliders will be extended by analyses of $B$-meson displaced vertices at Belle II, which can detect $K^+ \eta_1^{(m)}$ final states where the ALP decays invisibly. By combining these displaced vertex searches with the branching ratio limits from the oscillation studies, Belle II will effectively probe the $B$-meson mixing amplitude for ALPs across a broad mass range, from invisible decays up to $m=2$ GeV. Ultimately, these investigations will yield the most stringent constraints on $A(B\to\eta_1)$ to date, potentially rivaling the sensitivity of future neutrinoless double-baryon mixing searches. This paper details the strategies employed at Belle II to measure $B$-meson oscillations into ALPs and to search for displaced vertices arising from their invisible decays. It also outlines the anticipated limits on branching ratios and mixing amplitudes achievable at Belle II and compares them with projections from other proposed experiments. Finally, it discusses the implications of these limits for new physics models.

Semantic alteration detection (SAD) identifies changes in meaning between text pairs, a task crucial for applications like plagiarism detection, content safety filtering, and programmatic translation quality assessment. Although recent advances in neural methods for sentence and semantic similarity have made it possible to detect semantic alterations by comparing the representations of original and modified sentences, these approaches often lack explainability. This study investigates contextualized language models for unsupervised SAD, evaluating their performance against various baseline techniques. Our analysis reveals that contextualized models do not necessarily outperform simpler methods, such as edit distance, and that their effectiveness is highly dependent on the specific type of semantic change. Furthermore, we find that these models struggle with syntactic alterations that do not result in semantic shifts. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for future research in unsupervised semantic change detection. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/linguamatics/Contextualized_SAD.

We investigate the spin distribution of confirmed and candidate ultracompact objects, specifically black hole X-ray binaries and active galactic nuclei (AGNs), to determine if the superradiance mechanism can constrain the mass range of ultralight bosons. Our analysis indicates that observed high spins of black holes in both X-ray binaries and AGNs are unlikely to result from accretion alone, implying that superradiance must operate to limit the maximum spin and consequently constrain the boson's mass. Utilizing a direct measurement of the spin distribution for 21 black hole X-ray binaries and 30+ AGNs, we derive constraints on the boson mass commensurate with current experimental limits. Furthermore, we propose that the spin distribution of these ultracompact objects can help identify the particle responsible for dark matter within the ultralight boson mass range of $10^{-13}$ to $10^{-9}$ eV. This approach offers a direct method to explore the parameter space of axion-like and hidden photon models, which are otherwise difficult to investigate. Additionally, the spin distribution of black holes serves as a valuable probe for examining physics within the strong gravity regime.

We present a Monte Carlo approach for simulating the time evolution of driven quantum harmonic oscillators via the path integral formalism. This simulation enables the computation of expectation values for time-dependent operators. To achieve this, we employ a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to generate a sequence of Metropolis steps, which sample a discrete-time path integral representation of the system's time evolution operator. This sampling occurs over a discrete time grid across the continuous phase space. The resulting Monte Carlo samples of the path integral allow for the numerical evaluation of the time evolution operator and associated expectation values. We validate this method by calculating expectation values for various operators and comparing the results against known analytical solutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the approach's utility by computing the Wigner function and wavefunction for the quantum harmonic oscillator under different driving forces. The implementation of this method is available as an open-source Python package at https://github.com/Aditya-1999/PMC.

We introduce a calculus for quantum relational Hoare reasoning that integrates expectations, a concept from single quantum Hoare logic used to quantify side effects. This calculus enables reasoning about pairs of programs through a combination of relational and single program logic. We demonstrate the calculus's utility by defining a set of refinement rules for quantum expectations and a collection of rules for verifying quantum safety-critical properties. Furthermore, we establish the soundness of these refinement and verification rules within a semantic framework. Finally, we show how to derive a quantum relational Hoare logic for a Hoare variant of the language, a result that is of independent significance. To our knowledge, this work represents the first attempt to develop a calculus for quantum *relational* Hoare reasoning that incorporates side-effect quantification via expectations. The calculus serves as the foundation for a type-and-effect system for the same language, which is detailed in a companion paper. Our findings contribute to the field of quantum program verification. The source code for this work is accessible at https://github.com/quantum-verification/QRE-Expectations.

The vector magnetic field is a fundamental physical quantity essential for understanding solar atmospheric dynamics and for guiding the development of advanced solar forecasting models. These models rely on deep learning techniques to infer solar image data, which in turn drive data-driven simulations aimed at enhancing solar predictions. However, because these inference methods are trained on measured vector magnetic field data, any inherent biases in the measurements can be inadvertently learned and amplified by the models. This creates a significant challenge for data-driven solar forecasting. This study examines the distribution of line-of-sight (LOS) and azimuthal ($\phi$) angles across the solar disk within the HMI vector magnetic field data. We identify a bias in the inferred LOS and $\phi$ angles that correlates with the LOS field strength, a bias that is absent in the true measured LOS and $\phi$ angles. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this bias is not present in the true measured azimuthal angle. Finally, we propose a method to correct this bias in the inferred LOS and $\phi$ angles, which also adjusts the inferred vector field strength. The corrected data aligns more closely with the true measured LOS and $\phi$ angles and exhibits reduced variance in the inferred vector field strength. These findings indicate that the bias in the inferred LOS and $\phi$ angles—and consequently in the vector field strength—is a result of the inversion process rather than the underlying measurements. By addressing this bias, we can enhance the accuracy of deep learning models used to infer solar images for data-driven solar forecasting. The corrected data will be made available through the standard solar data pipeline. Ultimately, this work offers insights into the relationship between the true measured and inferred magnetic field quantities, helping to clarify the physical significance of the vector magnetic field. Additionally, it provides guidance for developing improved inversion techniques and refining deep learning-based inference methods for solar images to support data-driven solar forecasting. The analyses presented in this study are based on the Solar/Space Physics Community Coordinated Modeling Center (CME) model runs, which utilize the spectrally forward modeling radiative magneto-hydrodynamic (RHM) Bifrost code to simulate solar atmospheric images and the vector magnetic field inversion MeInVerF. These runs utilize the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) vector magnetic field data and $B\cdot n$ images from the Solar Orbiter/SPICE/UVSP instrument as inputs. Detailed descriptions of the data, inversion methods, and bias identification and mitigation strategies are provided in the main text and accompanying figures. This paper examines the boolean structure of $W(\Gamma)$, defined as the collection of involutions within a right-angled Coxeter group $W(\Gamma)$ associated with a graph $\Gamma$. We demonstrate that $W(\Gamma)$ forms a boolean algebra if and only if the graph $\Gamma$ is a complete multipartite graph. Furthermore, we analyze the boolean structure of $W(\Gamma)$ when $\Gamma$ is a tree, providing a characterization of the corresponding covering poset. As an application, we derive a lower bound for the size of the boolean algebra generated by the involution of an affine Weyl group.

This study examines timelike Bertrand curves within the context of semi-metric spaces, a framework that extends the classical Riemannian metric by introducing a semi-metric. We demonstrate that, similar to the case in Riemannian manifolds, the definition of a timelike Bertrand curve in a semi-metric space is not unique. Furthermore, we establish that a timelike curve in a semi-metric space qualifies as a Bertrand curve if and only if it is a circle or a slant helix. Finally, we provide a complete classification of these curves. The results indicate that, aside from circles, the only timelike Bertrand curves in a generic semi-metric space are slant helices characterized by a specific relationship between their curvature and torsion. In the special scenario where the curve is a slant helix with constant curvature and torsion, we derive its explicit parametric form. These findings suggest that, analogous to Riemannian manifolds, the concept of a Bertrand curve in a semi-metric space is most meaningful when the curve is a slant helix. As an application, we derive the parametric equations for a timelike curve in a generic semi-metric space to function as a Bertrand curve, given a specific regular timelike curve acting as its mate. The results herein are significant for the theory of curves in Riemannian and semi-metric spaces, particularly for the classification of special curves such as Bertrand and Chebychev curves. This work also holds potential value for applications in physics, including relativity and optics. Regarding methodology, the paper relies on standard concepts from differential geometry, including regular curves, Frenet frames, curvature, torsion, and geodesics. No new definitions were introduced, as all necessary concepts are well-established in the literature. For instance, the definition of a regular curve in a semi-metric space is identical to that in a Riemannian manifold, and the definition of curvature in a semi-metric space aligns with the standard definition used in Riemannian geometry. This study conducts a comprehensive analysis of the influence of loss function selection on the performance of deep learning models for image classification. The research evaluates seven distinct loss functions across three model architectures: ResNet-18, ResNet-34, and ResNet-50, utilizing two datasets: ImageNet and a specialized dataset for detecting COVID-19 in chest X-ray images. The evaluation criteria include accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC. The findings indicate that the Cross-Entropy loss function yields the highest accuracy on both datasets. Furthermore, the study observes that accuracy and F1-score are more strongly impacted by the choice of loss function than recall, with the Cross-Entropy function demonstrating superior performance in generating precise predictions. These results offer valuable insights for selecting an optimal loss function for specific image classification tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/Loss-Function-Analysis.

We introduce ATOMIC, an atlas of deep neural models trained on if-then reasoning tasks, which we refer to as hypothetical tasks. These tasks consist of textual inputs comprising a premise and a hypothesis, with the objective of classifying the hypothesis as entailed, neutral, or contradicted based on the premise. The models within the ATOMIC atlas were developed by various research groups using different architectures and approaches. Consequently, the atlas serves as a valuable resource for investigating the training, architecture, and performance of diverse models on hypothetical tasks. Furthermore, it acts as a testbed for new models, enabling the evaluation of their performance against a range of existing models. We anticipate that the atlas will be a useful tool for both academic research and industry applications, particularly for developing models capable of performing hypothetical reasoning. To support this, we have created an interactive website that allows users to explore the atlas and test new models. The website and the atlas itself are accessible at http://atomic.ai2.io/. The source code for the atlas and website is available at https://github.com/google/atomic. Additionally, we have released the data required to recreate the neural models in the atlas, along with the code to generate the data files used by the website, at https://github.com/google/atomic-data.

Video prediction remains a significant challenge, particularly for new view scenarios where the camera angle changes. In these situations, the scene undergoes both global transformations due to the shift in viewpoint and local changes caused by moving objects. This paper introduces a novel approach for new view video prediction that leverages a dual representation to separately address global and local dynamics. Our method begins by converting input videos into a dual representation composed of a global descriptor and a set of local descriptors. We then employ a global network to map the descriptor pair to a future global descriptor, which is subsequently transformed into a new view using a learned global transformation. Simultaneously, a local network predicts future local descriptors, which are also converted to the new view via the same learned transformation. Finally, a fusion network reconstructs the future video in the new view from both the predicted global and local descriptors. Extensive experiments on three new view video prediction datasets demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art results. The source code is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1998/Dual-Representation-For-New-View-Video-Prediction.

The metric dimension of a graph represents the smallest size of a resolving set, a concept extensively studied in recent literature. This paper introduces a new parameter called the trimmed metric dimension, defined as the minimum cardinality of a resolving set that includes all leaves. We establish tight upper and lower bounds for this parameter across various graph families and investigate its fundamental properties. Furthermore, we determine the exact value of the trimmed metric dimension for specific graph classes, including trees, cycles, and graphs with diameter three. Our analysis reveals that for trees, the trimmed metric dimension equals the number of leaves minus one, whereas for graphs with diameter three, it is at most half the total number of vertices. We also examine how this parameter behaves under standard graph operations. Additionally, we define a resolution index based on the cardinality of resolving sets and explore its relationship with the trimmed metric dimension. Finally, we characterize graphs where the trimmed metric dimension is one greater than the index of resolvability. Throughout this study, we demonstrate that the trimmed metric dimension is not monotonic with respect to inclusion. Our findings indicate that the trimmed metric dimension offers valuable insights into the structural characteristics of graphs.

Heart sounds serve as a vital indicator for diagnosing cardiovascular disorders, yet their analysis is complicated by the presence of additive noise and convolutional distortion. These issues are particularly severe in real-world scenarios, where ambient sounds and mechanical vibrations from cardiac monitors frequently degrade signal quality. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to address both additive noise and convolutional distortion in heart sound signals. The proposed method employs a two-stage approach: first, an additive noise pre-processing module cleans the signal, followed by a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier that categorizes heart sounds into normal and abnormal groups. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework effectively mitigates the adverse effects of both noise types. Furthermore, the model achieves state-of-the-art performance on a noisy heart sound dataset, yielding a 9.1% increase in F1-score compared to the current best method. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulrahmanAlshammari/HeartSoundCategorization.

We investigate the intensities of fine-structure transitions from neutral atomic carbon (C\textsc{ i}) in 19 star-forming galaxies, aiming to determine if these lines are over-luminous relative to the surrounding molecular gas reservoirs. By deriving the column densities of C\textsc{ i} from the C\textsc{ i}(1\rightarrow0) and (2\rightarrow1) lines and those of H$_2$ from the dust continuum, we calculated the ratios $n(\text{C\textsc{ i}})/n(\text{H}_2)$ for each galaxy. These values were then compared against a theoretical relation between these column densities and the ratio of molecular gas cooling from C\textsc{ i} to H$_2$, which is a function of density and chemical composition. For 17 galaxies, the $n(\text{C\textsc{ i}})/n(\text{H}_2)$ fell below the theoretical expectation, indicating that the C\textsc{ i} lines are sub-thermally excited within the molecular gas reservoirs. This excitation state is likely driven by the low densities ($n(\text{H}_2)<10^{22}$ cm$^{-2}$) and high gas-to-dust ratios ($\sim$80) characteristic of these reservoirs. Consequently, the C\textsc{ i} lines may be underutilized as tracers for low-density, extended molecular gas. Furthermore, we propose that the $n(\text{C\textsc{ i}})/n(\text{H}_2)$ ratio serves as a valuable metric for assessing the bulk density of molecular gas reservoirs, offering a simple method to identify galaxies with gas dominated by low-density reservoirs. Such identification is crucial for understanding the chemical composition of these reservoirs and optimizing the selection of appropriate tracers for future surveys, including the ATHENA project. Ultimately, the $n(\text{C\textsc{ i}})/n(\text{H}_2)$ ratio could act as a diagnostic tool for the bulk density of molecular gas in galaxies, complementing existing diagnostics like star formation efficiency and gas fraction. To facilitate this, we provide a simple fitting formula for the $n(\text{C\textsc{ i}})/n(\text{H}_2)$ ratio as a function of $n(\text{H}_2)$ and the C\textsc{ i}/H$_2$

We demonstrate that for ASEP with step initial conditions, the velocity process associated with a specific family of interfaces converges to a diffusion process governed by a skew Brownian motion with drift. This convergence holds true for both conservative and non-conservative dynamics. Furthermore, we establish that the velocity process fully characterizes the law of the interface, a result that extends to non-conservative dynamics as well. Finally, we show that the law of the ASEP with simple asymptotic initial conditions can be derived from the law of the corresponding stepped initial condition. As a direct application, we utilize these findings to determine the distribution of the height at the origin for ASEP governed by simple asymptotic initial conditions.

Mathematical models of infectious disease spread have been a significant area of research for over a century, driven by the need to understand outbreaks and evaluate control measures. While numerous models have been developed for various pathogens, there is no single universal framework; instead, a wide variety of approaches exist, each with distinct advantages and limitations. Selecting the appropriate model for a specific epidemic requires balancing theoretical goals with practical constraints, such as data availability, computational resources, and the intended use. In this paper, we provide an overview of common epidemiological models, illustrating their application to the current SARS-CoV-2 epidemic through concrete examples. We conclude by discussing future research directions and potential uses for modeling the ongoing epidemic and similar outbreaks. This review is not intended to be exhaustive; rather, it offers a snapshot of the field's current state, highlighting both the utility and the challenges inherent in modeling infectious diseases. Given the rapid evolution of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic, the urgency of implementing effective control strategies, and the emergence of new pathogens, mathematical models will remain essential for investigating outbreaks, assessing interventions, and guiding public health decisions.

The star formation rate (SFR) of massive galaxies appears to decline as they approach the truncation of the fundamental plane, a phenomenon potentially linked to central structural changes. While recent studies have proposed that bulge growth suppresses star formation in the surrounding disk, we challenge this view by demonstrating that the rise in specific star formation rate (sSFR) during bulge expansion is actually driven by a drop in sSFR within the disk. Furthermore, we find that the contribution of the central region to the total SFR is minimal, even in galaxies with the most prominent bulges. These results indicate that global structural components are unlikely to be the primary cause of the M*-SFR relation's turnover at high masses. Instead, we propose that physical processes operating on smaller scales—such as the regulation of gas inflow by the central black hole—are responsible for this turnover. To test this hypothesis, we will examine the correlation between NUV variability and the Eddington ratio in the most massive galaxies. This work represents a collaborative effort by the NUV variability team, with specific contributions from A.  Paolillo regarding the central region analysis. The datasets utilized in this study were generated by the Dark Energy Survey (DES), a project led by DOE's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. Additional data sources include the SDSS, GALEX, 2MASS, and Pan-STARRS1 surveys.
